extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism students, policy analysts, and researchers interested in news production, media law, and ideology
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating how news is produced, what constraints (legal, organizational, professional) shape access and content, and how news practices instantiate or mask ideology. Includes consideration of First Amendment issues, the Fairness Doctrine, professional norms, and interpretive sociological critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of access to media in determining truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions of access are embroiled in contemporary court cases involving the First Amendment; access to the media is important in the determination of truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contends that who gains access to media outlets (owners, licensees, professional networks) affects which ideas become established as truth; draws analogy to scientific communities where access to leading journals and professional networks shapes what is accepted as scientific truth (Kuhn, Mullins, Crane, Reskin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Newspapers as private property with owner editorial rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers are identified as private property, and those who own newspapers have the right to publish what they will; newspapers are not legally required to grant access to their pages to anyone who wants it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owner rights are subject to certain limitations (e.g., national security). The practical effect is that owners have the final word on how an issue will be handled; quote: 'Freedom of the press is guaranteed only to those who own one.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal distinction between owners and broadcast licensees
rubrics_metrics.description: Television and radio license holders are legally 'licensees' who hold a public trust, whereas newspaper proprietors are treated as private owners; the government directly regulates stations because of limited frequencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Networks are largely suppliers of programs and exempt from direct FCC regulation, but FCC can influence networks through stations/affiliates; sales of licenses require FCC approval though not selection of buyer. This distinction affects claims of First Amendment protection and access obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness Doctrine / Section 315 obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadcasters have an obligation to operate in the public interest and to afford reasonable opportunity for the discussion of conflicting views on issues of public importance (Section 315(a) and FCC rulings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 1961 FCC ruling stressed affirmative obligations: broadcast licensees must air programs devoted to public issues and must afford persons holding opposing viewpoints reasonable opportunity to present their views, especially where personal attacks on local officials occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professionalism as guarantor of fairness and objectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: News professionals claim that professional methods and practices (editing, fact assessment) guarantee a fair presentation and thus protect free speech without regulatory intervention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: NBC's defense of its documentary argued that professional practices, disclaimers, attempts to obtain rebuttals, and 'editing' suffice to ensure fairness; the professional claim serves to blur public/private distinctions and to resist regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chilling effect of regulation on newswork
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation (or the threat of being sued/regulated) produces a 'chilling effect' that makes journalists overly cautious and hampers news dissemination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Testimony (e.g., Walter Cronkite) argues reporters/editors must be free to fail without constant fear of legal or regulatory reprisal; organizations claim fairness rules inhibit necessary journalistic risk-taking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial discretion: 'editing is what editors are for'
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors exercise selection and choice of material; editing is an accepted professional responsibility even though editors sometimes abuse this power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice Burger's opinion notes that editing/selection is the remedy (insofar as it exists) against perceived abuse by editors, coupled with 'a spirit of moderation and a sense of responsibility—and civility.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational 'must' stories override news judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Both newspapers and television carry 'must stories' dictated by business offices, advertising staff, or management that editors must run, exempting them from normal competition among news items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalism pedagogy codifies the 'must' slug (Hohenberg): 'must' should be used only for stories that 'must' be run; such mandates indicate organizational constraints on professional discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sponsor/advertiser influence on story ordering and placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Sponsorship and advertiser relationships influence story ordering and placement to avoid uncomfortable juxtapositions between content and commercials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: when a bank or airline sponsors a newscast, newsworkers rearrange story order or commercial placement to avoid proximity of sensitive items (bank robberies, air crashes) next to related sponsor commercials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict between professional dominance and owner/manager control
rubrics_metrics.description: Professional claims to determine news and to be independent often conflict with owners and managers who may overrule news judgment for managerial or commercial reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by resignations or firings (e.g., Fred Friendly at CBS, editors fired at Pan-Ax chain), showing that professional autonomy is contingent and contested within organizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Web of facticity as professional construction of 'the true account'
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary journalism aspires to present 'the true account' through professional practices that assemble facts and include responsible parties; this 'web of facticity' defines factuality within journalism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practices include careful assessment of facts, attempts to contact and offer rebuttal time, and using professional standards to define what counts as validated fact; criticism: this frames 'right to know' as access to the facts established by professionals, not necessarily to all perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: News limits access and transforms dissent (news as ideology)
rubrics_metrics.description: News practices limit access to radical views and transform dissent by privileging ahistorical, concrete, and contingency-focused reporting that avoids structural analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that these practices legitimate the contemporary state, prevent analytic understanding of social conditions, and thereby limit the public's ability to ascertain truths and to organize for social change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideology substitutes concepts for reality (Smith)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideology 'makes the structure of society mysterious by substituting concepts for reality'—news presents terms like 'public' and 'private' as if they naturally described society, thereby hiding socioeconomic structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an analytical criterion: look for when news uses conceptual shorthand that closes off further inquiry into structural causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treating what ought to be explained as fact or assumption
rubrics_metrics.description: News often treats as given those aspects of society that ought to be explained, opting for concrete stories and present-time orientation over structural linkage and analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicator of ideological reporting: absence of analysis, emphasis on contingency and individual events, and dismissal of deeper structural explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideological procedures that prevent inquiry (temporal/spatial anchoring and professionalism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Temporal and spatial anchoring of the news net, together with professional framing, prevent certain events or analyses from being defined and disseminated as news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames label some analyses as 'soft-news' or dismiss them as irrelevant, thereby precluding inquiry into structural or systemic issues; professional norms act as filters that exclude some types of stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: News as constructed reality (interpretive approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: News does not simply mirror society; newsworkers and organizations actively define what is newsworthy, thereby constructing shared social reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under this approach, newsworthiness is negotiated moment-to-moment (e.g., editors deciding page-one items), and reporting shapes events' meanings (e.g., media constructing early images of social movements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Government intervention to encourage viewpoint diversity can blur public/private distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislation such as the Newspaper Preservation Act was designed to support failing newspapers to increase published viewpoints, raising the possibility that Congress could legislate readers' rights of access and thereby blur distinctions between private and public spheres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion highlights that regulatory responses to market failure may alter previously privatized editorial autonomy and prompt legal/political contestation over access rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous dependence of media 'truth' on professional networks (scientific analogy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Just as scientific truth depends on professional networks, publication norms, and access to leading journals, what is accepted as truth in media depends on organizational and professional arrangements that enable certain accounts to gain prominence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Kuhn, Mullins, Crane, Reskin to argue that advances/truths emerge from social organization and access, not a linear cumulative assessment of ideas; implication: evaluate media truth claims by examining access and network structures.
